records.current_summary:
South Atlantic island settlement with its own assembly: same-sex activity legal since 1989, equal age of consent since 2005, and full equality in April 2017 when the assembly approved same-sex marriage and civil partnerships 7-1, on a public consultation showing 90 per cent support for marriage and 94 per cent for partnerships — the registrar confirmed the law the following June, adoption followed the same year, the constitution bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and the first Pride was held in the capital that April. An official of the community described it as 'open, tolerant and respectful'; note that the much more remote dependencies administered from the same capital did not follow on marriage.

The earlier profile's inherited arithmetic and its borrowed UK custody stories have been deleted: on the surviving evidence the legal picture here is stronger, not weaker, than the administering state's, and there is no source indicating the GB single-sex-services code extends to the territory.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in the Falkland Islands (Wikipedia; Prisons Ordinance 2017 equal-treatment clause)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in the Falkland Islands' article documents no trans-prisoner housing data for the territory - no birth-sex vs identity placement policy, no special units, no solitary/segregation practice - but its hate-crime section notes that the Prisons Ordinance 2017 (legislation.gov.fk, in force 2019-07-17) requires prison staff to treat all prisoners equally without distinction to, among other categories, sexual orientation; a statutory equal-treatment clause covering prison staff, with no trans-specific placement or segregation detail.

records.current_summary:
A self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, Guernsey moved briskly through the 2010s: in 2011 it aligned blood-donation rules with the metropole, ending the HIV-era ban on gay and bisexual donors; in June 2015 the states rewrote the adoption law to open adoption to same-sex couples, removing a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples; and in December 2015 the states approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting civil-partnership and secular-union alternatives as insufficient, with the law itself commencing from spring 2018.

That record covers sexual orientation squarely; the position on gender identity was asserted in the earlier profile without any cited source and has been deleted, so a transgender visitor should treat legal gender recognition and trans-specific protection as unestablished here — the more notable local quirk being that, on the documented chronology, civil partnership arrived later than in the neighbouring dependency that shares the island group's institutions.

prison_adds.title: Guernsey Prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia article on Guernsey Prison (Les Nicolles), the island's only prison: opened 1989, 11 wings, capacity 139, operated by the States of Guernsey and accommodating male, female and vulnerable prisoners of juvenile and adult ages (population ~99 in November 2024). Contains no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special unit, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners; verdict thin: no usable finding on the prison-housing axis.

records.current_summary:
Ghana is dangerous for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for “promotion.” President Akufo-Addo refused to assent pending legal challenges, the Supreme Court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when the 8th parliament dissolved — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, “unnatural carnal knowledge” carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. Accra has a resilient underground community (LGBT+ Rights Ghana — whose 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.

prison_adds.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
prison_adds.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities; it proposes that identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer be punished by up to three years' imprisonment, adds a 'duty to report' prohibited acts to police, and was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. Establishes the direct state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone - the population to which any prison-placement practice would apply - while containing no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

prison_adds.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
prison_adds.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison sentences of three to 10 years - up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer for promotion/advocacy. Community groups (e.g. One Love Sisters Ghana) report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. The article contains no information on prison placement of trans prisoners, confirming the absence of any publicly documented housing policy for them in Ghana.

records.current_summary:
Greece is a workable destination with a clear law-versus-practice gap. The legal framework is among Europe's strongest — it ranks 7th on the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map, has banned conversion therapy and intersex infant surgery, has a hate-crime law covering gender identity, and legalised same-sex marriage in 2024 (the first Orthodox-majority country to do so). There are no trans-specific border or bathroom restrictions, and the government is progressive with an improving trajectory.

But the social reality lags the law. A mob of about 150 people assaulted two trans people in Thessaloniki; an European Court of Human Rights case documented police detention and mistreatment of trans sex workers; surveys show Greeks are markedly more avoidant of public LGBTI visibility than the EU average (63% avoid holding hands); and the UK Foreign Office has issued an LGBTQ travel warning for Greece.

Major tourist destinations — Mykonos, Athens's Gazi district, Thessaloniki — are welcoming; outside them the climate is rougher than the law suggests.

prison_adds.title: Φυλακές Κορυδαλλού: Τρανς κρατούμενες θα μεταχθούν για πρώτη φορά στη γυναικεία πτέρυγα (LiFO)
prison_adds.summary: LiFO (4 Dec 2021): four trans detainees were ordered transferred to the women's prisons of Korydallou (Athens) by decision of the General Secretary for Crime-Prevention Policy Sofia Nikolaou, after each had petitioned for transfer stating they identify and wish to be treated as women. The four (three Greek, one Bulgarian) had been held at Trikala and Corfu prisons, effectively isolated and treated inconsistently with their self-identified gender. First documented transfer of trans prisoners to a women's facility in Greece; it illustrates that default placement had followed the male facilities and that an on-request transfer route to women's facilities existed.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ rights in Greece — Correctional Facilities section (Wikipedia)
prison_adds.summary: Wikipedia's overview of Greek LGBTQ rights records under 'Correctional Facilities' that since 4 December 2021 trans women detainees, upon their request, may be relocated to correctional facilities for women — the policy change matching the Korydallou transfers reported by LiFO the same day. Placement thus starts from the registered sex, with a 4 Dec 2021 decision creating an on-request transfer route for trans women; the article documents no special trans units and no rule covering trans men's placement.

records.current_summary: Grenada demands real caution. The buggery law (10 years) remains on the books (no successful court challenge yet), though unenforced; no LGR; small community; tourist areas insulated.

prison_adds.title: Grenada Stakeholder Report for the UN Universal Periodic Review: LGBTIQ+ Rights (The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali, GrenCHAP)
prison_adds.summary: UN UPR stakeholder report (submitted 11 Oct 2024): because Grenada has no laws permitting legal gender change, 'the Government also prosecutes transgender women – who are considered legal men under the law.' The report provides no prison-specific housing/segregation detail, but it establishes the operative placement framework: a trans person's legal status, and so any correctional classification, follows registered/birth sex rather than gender identity. No special unit, solitary/segregation practice, or trans-prisoner housing case/ruling is documented for Grenada.

prison_adds.title: Grenada 2023 Human Rights Report (US State Dept)
prison_adds.summary: US State Dept 2023 report (pub. Feb 2024): Grenada's sole penitentiary, designed for about 200 persons, held 385 prisoners as of August 2023, including six women in a separate block; conditions were harsh due to gross overcrowding, with potable water in men's-block hallways but not cells. The report documents gendered blocks and general detention conditions but records no transgender-specific housing policy, special unit, or segregation practice, and no trans-prisoner cases or complaints.
